items.title: Rise of the Kakatiyas & the Line of Rulers
items.body:
## From feudatories to sovereigns

- The **Kakatiyas** (c. **1163–1323**) began as **feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and then the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani**, rising to power in the **Telangana** uplands.
- **Rudradeva (Prataparudra I)** declared **independent sovereignty in 1163**, recorded in the **Anumakonda (Hanamkonda) inscription**; from his reign inscriptions began to be issued in **Telugu** rather than Kannada.
- Capital shifted from **Hanamkonda (Anumakonda)** to **Orugallu (Warangal)**.

## Succession of major rulers

| Ruler | Reign | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) | c.1163–1195 | Founded sovereignty; Thousand Pillar Temple |
| Mahadeva | c.1195–1199 | Short reign |
| **Ganapati Deva** | 1199–1262 | Greatest ruler; delta expansion; Motupalli charter |
| **Rudrama Devi** | c.1262–1289 | Rare woman ruler; praised by Marco Polo |
| **Prataparudra II** | 1289–1323 | Last ruler; fell to the Tughlaqs (1323) |

- The Kakatiya royal emblem was the mythical bird **Garuda**; their tutelary goddess was **Kakati** (a form of Durga), from whom the family name is derived.
keyPoints: Kakatiyas ruled c.1163–1323 from Orugallu (Warangal), shifting from Hanamkonda (Anumakonda).
They began as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.
Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) declared sovereignty in 1163 (Anumakonda inscription); Telugu replaced Kannada in inscriptions.
Ruler order: Rudradeva → Mahadeva → Ganapati Deva → Rudrama Devi → Prataparudra II.
Royal emblem was Garuda; the family name derives from the goddess Kakati (a form of Durga).
items.mnemonic: Ruler chain 'Ru-Ma-Ga-Ru-Pra' = Rudradeva, Mahadeva, Ganapati, Rudrama, Prataparudra II.

items.title: Ganapati Deva & the Motupalli Charter
items.body:
## The greatest Kakatiya

- **Ganapati Deva (r. 1199–1262)** had the longest and most expansive reign, unifying the **Telugu-speaking lowland deltas of the Godavari and Krishna** with the Telangana uplands.
- He fortified the capital **Orugallu with a massive granite wall**, ramparts, moat and bastions.
- He created the man-made **Pakhal (Pakhala) Lake** for irrigation — part of the Kakatiya network of **'tanks' (reservoirs)** such as Laknavaram and Ramappa Cheruvu, many still in use.

## Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam

- At the port of **Motupalli** (modern **Prakasam district**) Ganapati Deva issued the **Abhaya Sasanam (charter of safety/'edict of fearlessness')**.
- It **guaranteed the safety of foreign merchants and their goods** and levied only a **fixed, moderate duty**, greatly encouraging maritime trade.
- The Motupalli inscription also traces the dynasty's mythical descent to the **solar line (Suryavamsa)**.
keyPoints: Ganapati Deva (1199–1262) was the greatest Kakatiya; extended rule to the Godavari–Krishna delta.
He walled Orugallu in granite and created the man-made Pakhal (Pakhala) Lake.
The Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam guaranteed safety and fixed low duties for overseas merchants.
Motupalli (Prakasam district) was the chief Kakatiya port.
Kakatiya 'tanks' (Pakhal, Laknavaram, Ramappa Cheruvu) pioneered upland reservoir irrigation.
items.mnemonic: Motupalli = 'Merchants Openly Trade, Under Protection' — the Abhaya (fearlessness) charter.
items.source: Motupalli inscription of Ganapati Deva; Andhra Pradesh Gazetteers; Eaton

items.title: Rudrama Devi & Marco Polo
items.body:
## A rare queen regnant

- **Rudrama Devi** (r. c. **1262–1289**) was **one of the very few women to rule as sovereign in medieval India**.
- She was married to **Virabhadra, an Eastern Chalukyan prince of Nidadavolu**, chosen by her father Ganapati Deva.
- She **repelled the invasions of the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri** and continued fortifying Orugallu, raising Ganapati's wall and adding an outer earthen wall and a wide moat.
- Having no son, she nominated her **grandson Prataparudra II** as heir.

## Marco Polo's testimony

- The Venetian traveller **Marco Polo** (visiting c. **1289–1293**) described her rule in **flattering terms**, praising the justice and prosperity of her realm.
- He called the kingdom **'Mutfili'**, a name derived from the port area around **Masulipatnam**, and noted its diamonds.
keyPoints: Rudrama Devi (c.1262–1289) was one of the few women sovereigns of medieval India.
She married Virabhadra, an Eastern Chalukya prince of Nidadavolu.
She repelled the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri and strengthened Orugallu's fortifications.
Marco Polo (c.1289–1293) praised her rule and called the kingdom 'Mutfili' (after Masulipatnam).
Lacking a son, she nominated her grandson Prataparudra II as successor.
items.mnemonic: 'Rudrama ruled, Marco marvelled at Mutfili' — links the queen to Marco Polo's port-name.

items.title: Prataparudra II & the Fall of Warangal
items.body:
## The last Kakatiya

- **Prataparudra II** (r. **1289–1323**) faced repeated invasions from the **Delhi Sultanate**.
- **1303** — an early Khalji foray was defeated by the Kakatiya army at the **Battle of Upparapalli**.
- **1310** — **Malik Kafur** (Alauddin Khalji's general) besieged and took Orugallu; Prataparudra was forced to pay **annual tribute**, and the famed **Koh-i-Noor diamond** is said to have passed to Delhi.
- **1318** — a further siege under **Khusrau Khan** compelled renewed submission.

## The end, 1323

- **1323** — **Ulugh Khan (Jauna Khan)**, son of Sultan **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq**, conquered Warangal after a long siege; Prataparudra was captured and is believed to have **died (suicide) near the Narmada** en route to Delhi.
- Orugallu was renamed **Sultanpur**, ending Kakatiya rule and ushering in a period of confusion in the Telugu country.
keyPoints: Prataparudra II (1289–1323) was the last Kakatiya ruler.
1310: Malik Kafur's siege forced tribute; the Koh-i-Noor is said to have gone to Delhi.
1323: Ulugh Khan (Jauna Khan), sent by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, finally conquered Warangal.
Orugallu was renamed Sultanpur after 1323.
Prataparudra reportedly died near the Narmada while being taken prisoner to Delhi.
items.mnemonic: Three sieges '10-18-23' (1310, 1318, 1323) — the third one ended the dynasty.

items.title: Kakatiya Art, Ramappa Temple & UNESCO 2021
items.body:
## Kakatiya architecture

- The Kakatiyas evolved a distinctive style: star-shaped platforms, **polished black dolerite** door-jambs and pillars, and **light 'floating bricks'** for the towers (vimanas).
- Landmark monuments: the **Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda** (Rudradeva, 1163), **Warangal Fort** with its ornamental **Kakatiya Kala Thoranam** (Kirti Torana — now the emblem of Telangana), and the **Ramappa Temple**.

## Ramappa (Rudreshwara) Temple

- Located at **Palampet (Mulugu district)**, built in **1213** by **Recherla Rudra**, a general (mahasamanta) of **Ganapati Deva**; dedicated to Shiva as **Rudreshwara**.
- Uniquely named after its **sculptor/architect Ramappa**.
- Engineering marvels: **floating-brick** superstructure and a **sand-box foundation** giving earthquake resistance; dolerite bracket-figures retain a **mirror polish after 800 years**.
- Inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021** (44th session), officially the **'Kakatiya Rudreswara (Ramappa) Temple'** (List No. 1570). Marco Polo reputedly called it 'the brightest star in the galaxy of temples'.
keyPoints: Kakatiya style: floating bricks for towers, polished dolerite carvings, star-shaped platforms.
Ramappa (Rudreshwara) Temple, Palampet — built 1213 by Recherla Rudra, general of Ganapati Deva.
It is uniquely named after its sculptor Ramappa; famed for its sand-box (earthquake-resistant) foundation.
Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 (44th session), List No. 1570.
Other monuments: Thousand Pillar Temple (Hanamkonda), Warangal Fort, Kakatiya Kala Thoranam (Telangana emblem).
items.mnemonic: Ramappa = 'temple named after the artist' + UNESCO 2021.

items.title: Musunuri Nayakas & the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
items.body:
## Musunuri Nayakas — post-Kakatiya resistance

- After 1323 the Telugu country fell into confusion under Delhi's governors. The **Musunuri Nayakas**, claiming **Kakatiya heritage**, led the resistance.
- **Prolaya Nayaka** rose at **Rekapalle (near Bhadrachalam)** c. 1330 and issued the **Vilasa (copper-plate) grant**, lamenting the devastation of the Telugu land and posing as the restorer of order. He left no children.
- His cousin **Kapaya Nayaka (r. 1333–1368)** led a wider revolt and **recovered Warangal from the Tughlaq governor Malik Maqbul in 1336**, aided (per the Kaluvacheru grant) by **75 Nayakas** and the Hoysala **Veera Ballala III**.
- Kapaya took the title **'Andhra Suratrana'** (Sultan of the Andhra country) but lost ground (including **Golconda**) to the **Bahmanis**, and was finally killed by the rival **Recherla Nayakas** at Bhimavaram in **1368**.

## Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (background)

- The **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** (coastal Andhra) were founded by **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** c. **624 CE**.
- Their king **Rajaraja Narendra** patronised **Nannaya**, the 'Adi Kavi', who began the **Telugu Mahabharatamu**.
- The Chalukya–Chola marital union produced **Kulottunga I**, who ascended the imperial Chola throne — merging the two lineages.
keyPoints: Musunuri Nayakas led post-Kakatiya Telugu resistance, claiming Kakatiya heritage.
Prolaya Nayaka (Rekapalle, near Bhadrachalam) issued the Vilasa grant c.1330.
Kapaya Nayaka recovered Warangal from Malik Maqbul in 1336 with 75 Nayakas and Hoysala help.
Kapaya took the title 'Andhra Suratrana' and was killed by the Recherla Nayakas in 1368.
Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi: founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana (c.624); Rajaraja Narendra patronised Nannaya; the Chola union produced Kulottunga I.
items.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musunuri_Nayakas; Vilasa Grant (Epigraphia Indica); History & Culture of the Andhras
